correctness.rationale: For a regular p-group the elements killed by p form Omega_1, so an exponent greater than p forces Omega_1 to be proper. The hypotheses of the published odd-prime second-maximum theorem therefore apply to every non-exponent-p regular group. Substituting the index-p upper bound on Omega_1 into the published cyclic-subgroup inequality gives exactly M_{p,n}, and the published equality condition reduces to exp(G)=p^2 and [G:Omega_1(G)]=p. For n<=p, the standard class bound cl(G)<=n-1 and Hall's class-less-than-p regularity theorem cover every p-group. For the wreath product, direct multiplication shows that outside the base an element has order p exactly when its coordinate sum is zero and otherwise order p^2; the resulting element-order count gives the displayed cyclic-subgroup formula and the positive difference from M_{p,p+1}.

Classical regular-p-group theory says the set of elements of order dividing p is Omega_1 and that class less than p implies regularity; this supplies a structural reduction, not an already-stated cyclic-subgroup extremum.

originality.rationale: The 2020 source proves the bound only under Omega_1(G) != G, explicitly leaves the p>=5, Omega_1(G)=G branch open, and mentions only the class-two obstruction. The present claim removes all regular p-groups, obtains a complete all-groups cutoff n<=p, and proves that cutoff sharp with an exact general count for C_p wr C_p. Statement-level searches across regularity, nilpotency class, Omega_1, second maxima, and wreath-product cyclic subgroup counts did not locate this combined theorem or the general wreath count.
residual_risks: An equivalent sharp-cutoff observation may exist under older regular-p-group terminology or in unindexed literature.
The general cyclic-subgroup count for C_p wr C_p is elementary enough that it may have been recorded without appearing in targeted searches.
The claim does not solve the open problem beyond the regular range; at order p^(p+1) the wreath product is only a lower-bound witness.
Search failure is not a proof of novelty.

value.rationale: The result resolves a natural, non-arbitrary initial range of a published second-maximum problem for every odd prime: all orders p^n through the largest range where regularity is forced. The cutoff n=p is mathematically intrinsic and is shown sharp by an explicit group at the next order. For p>=5 this removes every order below p^(p+1) from the unresolved branch, while the wreath calculation quantifies exactly how the regular extremal value first fails. This is a meaningful finite cutoff and structural boundary, not a routine isolated computation.
